LBNL Report #2001653 5.5 Statistics, model selection, and model evaluation The capture and processing of complimentary ancillary data that describes the context in which a radiation measurement is being made is the core technique underlying the SDF technology. However often optimally leveraging that context requires additional information that the sensors alone cannot readily provide. Do I know what isotope or spectral signature I am looking for? Do I know whether I am interested in a point-like source or a distributed source? Are sources surficial or being emitted from an attenuating medium? SDF algorithms have already been customized such that an experienced operator can preemptively configure the software to directly address the three questions above. But there are presently no mechanisms for the SDF software to automatically selectamodel,norhastherebeenintegratedgoodness-of-fitalgorithmsthatcouldautomatically(or guide a user to) select another algorithm configuration that would be better suited to a particular CONOP, or that would better describe the measurement. Additional research has shown how effectively prior information can constrain SDF reconstructions [75, 57]. A framework wherein spatial priors that are relevant for a particular use case a pre-generated and then applied to the contextual data and fit against measurements could result in dramatically improved performance of SDF systems with regard to ‘time-to-fit’ metrics. The simplest such framework would be deciding between point-like and unconstrained distributed sources. A more complex example would be to use lidar-observed duct and pipe dimensions to determinethemaximumdimensionsofpotentialhold-up, andtogenerateasuiteofscaledpotential hold-up configurations such as uniform, annular, and highly non-uniform lump, that could be fit based on the observed radiological data and measurement geometry. The primary reason that developing geometric specific source model templates could be so impactful is that it is an opportunity to put significant constraints on a SDF reconstruction. For example, a measurement of a residential neighborhood that is 100 m x 50 m with ≈ 20 single- and two-story buildings produced 1.7 million occupied 10-cm voxels, each of which becomes a free parameter in the SDF analysis attributing observed radioactivity. If the number of free- parameters was reduced to just those describing a handful of potentially relevant models, the measurements would be able to more rapidly describe the entire scene. However, the ability to quantify the uncertainty associated with the reconstruction when using such constrained models in paramount, and it is important to consider the possibility that incorrect assumptions/priors will produce incorrect results. The ability to perform model fits, model fit comparisons and to produce associated uncertainty maps would be impactful. Being able to create and fit such models in real- time may be computationally difficult. Creating a user interface that elucidates and enables model selection would also be needed.
